topics.chapterTitle: Appendix B — Executable Ownership and Failure Labs
topics.title: Requirement and model
topics.summary: A lease must release an acquired resource exactly once, including during exception unwinding. A failed acquisition must not be counted as a live lease. Moving a lease must transfer responsibility without duplicating it, and move assignment must first release the destination’s previous resource. Repeated explicit close must be harmless under this class’s contract.

blocks.text: The registry is a deterministic fake device with eight slots. It is not a wrapper around an operating-system handle API. Its counters make acquisition and release visible without relying on allocation addresses or external state. The registry owns the bookkeeping and must outlive every lease that borrows it. The lease owns responsibility for one slot, not the registry itself.

topics.title: Evidence and interpretation
topics.summary: The initial scope tests ordinary destruction. The next scope throws PlannedFailure only after acquisition, proving that a completed lease is destroyed during unwinding. The acquisition-rejection test throws a different type before a resource is obtained. The counters therefore distinguish a failed constructor from a successfully constructed object that later leaves scope.

blocks.text: Move construction leaves the source without a resource. Move assignment releases the destination’s previous slot before adopting the source’s slot. Do not generalize its handle reuse or failure behavior to a particular operating system without examining that API.

topics.chapterTitle: Appendix B — Executable Ownership and Failure Labs
topics.title: Practice boundary
topics.summary: Add a registry operation that reports a simulated completion failure while still consuming ownership. Decide whether retry is permitted. Then separate explicit completion from fallback cleanup and test both. Keep the registry alive throughout every lease scope. Do not “test” the borrowed lifetime by destroying the registry early and dereferencing it afterward; that would invoke a defect rather than verify a valid contract.

topics.chapterTitle: Appendix B — Executable Ownership and Failure Labs
topics.title: Requirement and model
topics.summary: Assigning a sequence must either produce an independent copy of the source values or leave the destination values unchanged. Copying can fail after zero, one, or two elements have been copied. The test uses a copy budget, not actual memory exhaustion, to make those failure points reproducible.

topics.chapterTitle: Appendix B — Executable Ownership and Failure Labs
topics.title: Evidence and interpretation
topics.summary: Assignment first constructs a private candidate from the source. If any cell copy throws, the partially constructed candidate is cleaned up and the destination has not been touched. With the default allocator used here, swapping the vector storage supplies the nonthrowing commit. The old destination then belongs to the local candidate and is destroyed on return.

blocks.text: The test repeats all three selected failure points, compares both source and destination snapshots, and then performs a successful assignment. Mutating the copied destination’s first value must not change the source. topics.summary: Add a second independently failing member to the destination type. Trace whether the combined assignment still has one nonthrowing publication point. topics.chapterTitle: Appendix B — Executable Ownership and Failure Labs
topics.title: Evidence and interpretation
topics.summary: The vector begins with reserved storage for three elements and then reserves beyond its current capacity. This forces a capacity increase without relying on an implementation’s growth factor. The program prints the observed copy and move counts for the current compiler/library combination. Different valid implementations may make different choices within their contracts, so exact counts are not fixture expectations.

blocks.text: The second part tests a direct move of the potentially throwing type. That type checks its rejection policy before changing the source value. Consequently, the failed direct move preserves the source under this class’s design. A later successful move sets the source value to zero. These outcomes are properties of the code in front of you, not a general promise that every throwing move preserves its source or every successful move empties it.

topics.chapterTitle: Appendix B — Executable Ownership and Failure Labs
topics.title: Evidence and interpretation
topics.summary: Two readers copy the owner of revision one. Replacing the current pointer publishes revision two for future readers but leaves revision one alive for the existing readers. Releasing the first reader is insufficient to expire the weak observer. Releasing the final strong reader allows expiry, and locking the expired observer produces no owner.

Resetting the ordinary snapshot pointer does not destroy the enclosing object because the aliasing owner remains. The stored pointer and the owned object’s address need not be identical; ownership identity and exposed address are distinct concepts.

The snapshot’s immutable layout makes the chosen member relationship straightforward. A mutable container would need a separate invalidation analysis.
